question: Google has recently announced that it is testing new solutions for its search results, including a new layout for its search engine results page, new refinement options and rich web results. In doing so, it appears that Google’s solutions may primarily benefit large online travel intermediaries by giving them even more visibility and increased organic traffic at the expense of European hotels’ own websites.

This will lead to less choice for consumers, fewer direct bookings for hotels and increased intermediation costs in a sector that is mostly made up of SMEs and is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic. Against this backdrop, in the Commission’s view: 1.

Are these changes compliant with the Digital Markets Act1, as regards both Art. 6(5) and the wider goals of the DMA, such as the fairness and contestability of digital markets for all business users of Google (hotels and online travel intermediaries alike)?

Is strengthening the visibility of Booking.com, which the Commission has classed as a dominant company for competition law purposes and which meets the gatekeeper criteria under the DMA, in line with the DMA’s overall objectives?

Is there sufficient awareness of the economic impact that the proposed changes will have on European hotels, many of which are SMEs or start-ups, and which are still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic?
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector, OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, p. 1.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.5.2024) Article 6(5) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA)1 aims at ending unfair self-preferencing practices by gatekeepers and ensure level playing field in the Digital Single Market. It bans gatekeepers from treating its own services and products more favourably, in ranking, indexing and crawling, than similar services or products of third parties.

Article 6(5) of the DMA also requires that ranking shall be transparent, fair and non-discriminatory. The Commission received Google’s compliance report on 7 March 2024. The Commission also organised a compliance workshop on 21 March 2024 where Google presented its proposed solutions, and third parties provided their comments.

On 25 March 2024, the Commission opened a non-compliance case against Alphabet on the suspicion that it is not complying with Article 6(5) of the DMA. The Commission is now investigating this issue as matter of priority. In its investigation, the Commission is gathering information from all stakeholders and will ensure proper consideration of all interests at stake, including the European hotel sector.

Since the designation of Google, the Commission has had numerous meetings (including bilateral meetings and workshops) with European hotels and their associations, including associations of small and medium enterprises. The Commission is therefore aware of the particularities of the European hotel sector.

In its assessment of Alphabet’s compliance with Article 6(5) of the DMA the Commission will also ensure that no specific group of stakeholders, including Booking.com, receives unjustified advantages. On 1 March 2024 Booking.com notified to the Commission its potential gatekeeper status under the DMA. The Commission has 45 days to assess the notification and possibly designate Booking.com. If Booking.
com is designated, it will then have to comply with all the obligations of the DMA within 6 months from its designation.
